full_text:
Interviewer:	It’ll probably be helpful for me to tell you a bit about what we’re doing. Basically we’re looking at women engineering students, we’re looking at people that are going on their placement but to see what their expectations of the placements are and how that might change when they’re actually on placement. But we also want to interview people that aren’t going on placement to find out why they don’t want to go on the placement – is there any particular reason or anything like that. Then, what we’re ultimately looking to do is improve women’s conditions in engineering and to see what we can do to increase numbers and see what we can do to help retain women in the industry. So I’ll just start by asking you a few backgrounds questions about why you decided to do it. Are you doing the…?

No, because I decided not to do it. I did put myself down

Interviewer:	For the placement?

Yeah.

Interviewer:	What course is it that you’re doing again?

I’m doing er air transport management

Interviewer:	Right, that was it – it just went out of my head for a minute. Right, what ‘A’ levels did you do?

I did maths, chemistry, geography and English.

Interviewer:	OK, and what type of school did you go to?

What do you mean?

Interviewer:	It wasn’t private or it wasn’t a girls’ schools or anything?

No, no, it was just a normal Catholic School.

Interviewer:	Ok, have you got any previous work experience?

Yes – I’ve got – let me just think through my 3 – erm the one time, during GCSE time I’ve gone 2 weeks work experience, at a bank, and I was banking and then I’ve gone 2 weeks working with [organisation] with their Head of Department. And the other one’s like a 3 day tour around [airport], and yeah, it took me ages to find that, but 2 years work, never mind. Yeah, so a 3 day course where I was taught air traffic control. (And I work as well?)

Interviewer:	OK. What do your parents do at all, are they in the industry at all?

No. Well, my dad’s in construction, in a company so…

Interviewer:	So, he is in the engineering industry but– not in your field. Why do you think that you decided to study Air Transport Management then?

It’s a long story (laughter). I’ve always wanted to work in like just planes and stuff – they just fascinate me. I think mostly it’s the airports that fascinate me, so I just wanted to work in an airport whatever happened, so I thought I’d just take this degree because I was gonna do air traffic control, but because I didn’t pass the exams, I had to come to uni. I only had 2 options after ‘A’ levels. I said either – ‘cos I only applied to one uni – this was the only one I applied to - I said, if I get in, I get in, if I don’t, I don’t. And er, I applied for air traffic control – I failed that and erm looking into this, afterwards, I got into uni. So I thought I might as well.

Interviewer:	Did you consider doing aeronautical engineering?

No. No I don’t like physics.

Interviewer:	What other factors do you think influenced your decision to do that? Did you have any careers advice or…?

I did. I er, I had a like – I thought about quite a lot of careers to go into but obviously airport was my interesting bit, so I thought. I did consider like doing marketing or I was going to do speech language therapy (oh right). I wanted to go to NHS, somewhere like that. And I also had er logistics as part of it, and that’s about it. (OK, so...) Nothing to do with engineering.

Interviewer:	How did you decide not to go with them things, in the end?

I got input from my personal tutor at my ‘A’ levels. He used to help me quite a bit and I – I used to sit there, after school, basically just slobbing around, going oh, I don’t know what to do and that, so that’s why I chose standard subjects in ‘A’ levels, ‘cos maths, English, geography, is like just general subjects. So I didn’t do anything specific except chemistry in case I would go into that but I didn’t think I’d ever go in that. (OK) And then I had my support from my family. That was – in our culture we’re not allowed – girls are not allowed to travel and it’s like, obviously after marriage – and it’s like a girl thing, isn’t it? Like ladies don’t travel, they get married and have (?) nice life – but er, I had the support from my parents and stuff and they said you can do whatever you want.

Interviewer:	OK – that helped?

Yeah, it did help. Like, it didn’t like draw me back and at least that pushed me forward.

Interviewer:	OK, how did you decide not to do the sandwich course? Why did you think that you didn’t want to do that?

Well, I’ve been applying – since I started Uni, I’ve been applying for placements since then, even that 3 day experience that I got from [airport], it took me 2 years, because I applied first and they said no to me, and I applied again. I wrote them a letter and said, I really want to do it (yeah) and its been the second time, I’ve been turned down, can you please give it to me. So that’s why I got it but I thought from my first experience I start from the beginning. So I started writing around and stuff, like looking around, seeing if I could find them and I had no luck. I had written about 60 letters so far and I didn’t get any replies. I think I’ve only got 8 replies out of that, and they’re all nos – so… I did – ‘cos I really wanted to do a placement, out of the UK – not the UK, but I wouldn’t mind abroad, in the EU, or like out of London, because that’s where I come from and I didn’t want to stay in London at all, so I thought Glasgow, Edinburgh, somewhere like that – anything like that but not London because I didn’t want to stay there. So erm, but I didn’t get any luck because I did apply abroad and none of them – they all said no to me. I don’t know why, but…I think it’s just September 11th thing – that is what affected it, because when I started my course, that’s when it happened, so that was a factor – but I thought, in 5 years time terminal 5 will come on so I thought that’s the time I’ll come out of uni and I’ll be ready, so I thought I’ve still got a chance.

Interviewer:	Did you think that’s because your course is quite specific? There’s only so many airports that you can apply to. Were you seriously tempted to think of placements?

No, not really, because the course that we do is so wide, like we do all the subjects in it. Like it’s not just airline or airports or anything, it’s everything. You know it’s got logistics in it, it’s got economics and it’s like generally all transport, because we do road transport. It’s not just airline – it’s just the name thats airline. Yeah, ‘cos it’s not just airlines. I probably could have gone into logistics if I’d really wanted, because I’m considering doing that because first year, when I started I was going to change the course because I thought it was too airline orientated but afterwards all the modules are different, so I thought it’s fine – I can then chang to transport and logistics. Because I like logistics – I do really well in that one, so..I thought I’d do that but no, I didn’t change – I thought I’d just keep to airlines.

Interviewer:	Have other people on your course – have they got placements then?

I don’t know. I have asked around and I think a few – they’re still applying because apparently it – you get the placement in summer, you don’t get it before or anything else, because nowadays everything’s coming in late, so yeah. I don’t know. I’ve heard a few have got it but I’m not too sure. They’ve all gone for interviews and stuff like that.

Interviewer:	Erm, why did you only want to come to [this university] then?

Well first this was the only – when I applied for this course, this was the only Uni that did airlines. (Really?) Or anything to do with airlines. The others weren’t really doing that course. It was just transport so – because obviously firstly, I was into airlines, so this was the only course – this wasn’t [name] university but that wouldn’t let me go in because I’d have to do – I’d either have to have 3 years experience in it, or I’d have a degree first and then go into that degree again. So erm I couldn’t – this was the only uni, so I thought I’d just take the risk. So that’s why I joined them.

Interviewer:	OK. Engineering generally is quite male dominated – is it the same in the air transport industry?

I’m not too sure. At the moment it’s – like air traffic control, is all male dominated. Like when I first started researching and now it’s changed, it’s got more ladies in it. I think everything’s changing now. It’s like being equal and everything, so it’s alright like that but it’s so – like in air traffic control, you – males get like successful and something like that.

Interviewer:	Did that bother you at all when you were applying?

No, it didn’t. I really wanted to do something different. I think the other thing ‘cos now I’m doing my community stuff – air transport, that’s like a big thing. It’s like I’m the only one doing this course and everyone’s like why? That’s something new isn’t it? So really, I like to be different, so I thought I’d apply to – I’m not fussed about if I was working with male colleagues and stuff like that.

Interviewer:	What about on your course, what are the gender proportions?

In that we’ve got like – I think we’ve only got 15 girls – the rest are males and we’ve got 50 people. It is quite low.

Interviewer:	Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering or your sort of subjects?

Well it depends on their interest really, but yeah. I don’t think it’s – there’s any problem in going in it cos’ its male dominated or cos’ they succeed in it or anything – that’s nothing to do with it, its just your (lost words) at the end of the day.

Interviewer:	Why do you think there aren’t more women in the industry?

Probably like in terms of convenience, isn’t it? ‘cos like that’s what I say that – if I got married, I obviously can’t fly (yeah). If I wanted to be an air hostess, I’d probably have to leave that or a pilot, that would be something that I couldn’t do. I’d have to be liked be based at one place wherever, I think that’s one (they can change though?). I guess that is different for every culture but I’d have to like – for me to move around, a lot would be a problem, so it’s stuff like that.

Interviewer:	OK, yeah. Do you think that there’s anything particularly that could be done to encourage more women into the industry?

Er, I don’t know.

Interviewer:	How did you find out about the industry in the first place?

I did do a lot of research, before I did get into – and I did a lot of – I’ve done – I’ve travelled quite a bit so that’s where I got my fascination from, in the first place and I’ve travelled quite a bit.

Interviewer:	Do you think that like in secondary schools, people should be provided with more information about…?

That is definite because when I started doing this – like my school didn’t even know about this course, and they didn’t know this thing existed in the first place, I must admit. Because they said out of all that – I think they were established for about 100 years – no student came out with it. I was the only one, so he was struggling but – ‘cos he lived in [place] and he worked at [name] Airport, and his wife was a teacher too, so he had a connection with [name] Airport, that’s why he knew about it. But like other teachers have no – not a clue that this course was even available or anything. I reckon – yeah, there is a lack of like information like I suppose. Because you get accounting and you get maths and you get all these chemistry and medical science and I think, engineering – in terms of engineering, you probably get mechanical engineering and stuff like that – building, but you wouldn’t get in terms of transport, they wouldn’t – I think, I guess it’s just a new thing now that’s just come up now, but you don’t really get information like that. Because I struggled – because obviously it was my research, that I did, with the help from my tutor, that I did get to this stage, but I wouldn’t have got to this stage because school didn’t have any information. I did it all on my own.

Interviewer:	Ok, what characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

(laughs) I think definitely you need to be imaginative, because you need imagination – like if you go into architecture, or whatever – construction, you need your brains like – in terms of like imagining stuff and like new things. I think you need that – definite – and you need erm and I think you also need your will power because if you don’t have that you can’t really – because like you’ve got so much competition around, obviously its still seen as a male dominated area – you have to – to get your point through you still have to like come up with something really good and I guess it is like – if you’ve got that interest and stuff you’d probably succeed in it. Not really do anything else. I think it’s them kind of characteristics that are – basically – I think you need more of it, ‘cos you’ve got that…

Interviewer:	Things like you need to work harder to prove yourself?

That’s it – to prove yourself. Yeah, you definitely need to prove it – that you can do it.

Interviewer:	Do you think there are any particular advantages or disadvantages of being a woman engineer?

Hmm, not really because it’ll be the same for every industry, I guess, because obviously like in computers, which are like male dominated, and like really you’ve got to hang on in there, so I think it’ll be the same probably.

Interviewer:	OK, I’m just going to ask you a few questions about your actual course. Is the course what you expected it would be?

At first I didn’t – I was not happy with it. I did consider to change it. But not changing in a sense from transport, just changing in terms of air transport ‘cos it’s a – ‘cos I didn’t have any luck in finding placements and stuff like that and it’s a bit hard. I thought I might have problem in finding a job later, because I was doing a degree to find a job later and if I don’t get anything then there’s no point. But now, now that I’m well into it, I’m quite happy with the course – it’s not, it’s everything I expected now, whereas like before we were like – ‘cos you don’t expect anything other than airlines or airports or air traffic and we had to do like roads and we had to do the vehicles and I was like oh no, I don’t know anything about cars –even though I drive a car. And stuff like that. It’s just like – you didn’t – you didn’t expect stuff like that. I didn’t expect logistics. I didn’t expect stuff like that – like economics. ‘Cos I used to hate economics and I was like oh no, it’s come back to haunt me. But yeah – now I don’t think it is – I like the fact that they’ve done it like that. It’s really good.

Interviewer:	What do you think has been the best and worst things about your course?

Er, I think the best bit is having 50% course work, 50% exams, I think I’d rather do more course work than exams. I like that. The worst thing is we have do 12 modules a year. ‘Cos it means that I – even though it’s not especially hard, we’re doing 10 different subjects a year and it’s just so much ‘cos like at [name] uni they do 8 a year and that’s 4 each semester, we do 2 more than them and it’s just so much. And it’s like sometimes with our six exams a term and it just gets too much after it. I think they’re trying to compact so much in a year and if they could increased the – I think people would be happy to do like a 4 year course, rather than a 3 year course and getting everything stuffed in there. But I guess it’s a fun part of learning, isn’t it? But I don’t like the fact that we do 12 modules – not too keen on that.

Interviewer:	Are you pleased that you did choose to come on this course?

I am. I have no doubts. I was saying this to my Mum yesterday, I have no doubts as to why I did this course or anything. I am happy. I think it will be hard to get in, but once you get in you’re just laughing because working in (?) you know where you’re going. You can find your way through upwards, wherever you want to go so I think once you get in, well it’s hard for every industry – it’s hard getting in I suppose. I don’t think it’s that different to anything else like – people make it out that it’s so different but it’s not – I think it’s the same.

Interviewer:	Do you think that people make out it’s so different probably just because they don’t actually know what it really is?

Yeah. And like the other thing is you’re actually, physically doing something, like you’re building something or you know, on the construction side or something. That’s about the only difference really or you’re wearing a helmet instead of having a suit or something – that’s the only difference but it’s – I think it’s just the environment that’s different. It’s nothing else really.

Interviewer:	OK, have you been taught by any female lecturers?

No. 

Interviewer:	None at all?

No.

Interviewer:	Erm, do you find that at all discouraging?

Erm, no.

Interviewer:	Or would you find it encouraging if you did have female lecturers?

I shouldn’t say this, but no, I’d rather have males.

Interviewer:	Why?

Ern, I don’t know. I’ve always noticed that females are a bit – a bit, I don’t know how to say it but – I don’t know. I find that…

Interviewer:	Is that like from your past experience? Do you think that men probably make better teachers?

Yeah – I think – well I don’t say better teachers or anything but I guess in terms of our industry I think I’d trust a male lecturer more than a female one. I guess it comes back to the fact that male are dominating again – do you get it? But I don’t know. No, I’ve never assumed I’d be taught by a – like a female, because you’ve always got this image that – from like ages that lecturers are all male. So you’ve always got to have – I’ve never had a female lecturer.

Interviewer:	Have you got a personal tutor?

Yeah, I do.

Interviewer:	Are they male or female?

Male

Interviewer:	Are they approachable?

Yeah. They’re approachable.

Interviewer:	Are you happy having a male for your tutor?

Yeah – definite.

Interviewer:	OK, has there been anything, or anyone who has been the biggest influence on you since you started your degree, would you say?

What do you mean, like in terms of my life?

Interviewer:	In terms of yeah – academically. Has there been a person or an event that’s happened, or anything like that?

I guess my personal tutor has really helped me greatly. That’s good. At first I was finding it really hard ‘cos it’s different to move all the way from home and stuff. And before I used – I was just like a – I don’t know what you’d call me. Probably one of those really quiet people, so I had to come out of that (yeah) and to be able to do like I say, to be really big step for me. I would say my personal – in terms of like lectures, or in terms of like Uni, I think my personal tutor. Then I also have so much support from my friends and stuff, so…

Interviewer:	Does that help?

Yeah, that’s what really helps. Unless you’ve got a really – I’ve got a really good mate. He’s like helped me so much and it shows in my results – definite. I’ve like improved by 10%.

Interviewer:	That’s really good. Have you had to do much group work at all?

No, but this year it has been quite a lot. Like this semester I’ve been doing group work, all the time. So I think I’ve got 3 that I have to do group work in. 

Interviewer:	Have you chosen yourself who you want to work with or were you just put in groups?

Oh one of them I was put in groups but the others, yeah, you can choose whoever you want to work with.

Interviewer:	Do you prefer working with other women or men or aren’t you bothered?

I’m not bothered like that, I’m not really fussed but I stick to one of my best mates on the course at the moment, so I like stick to her quite a bit and then we just pick the boys. ‘Cos we don’t really have a lot of girls on our course anyway. And the girls that we’ve got – I’m not too keen on, so I probably just stick to the clever people.

Interviewer:	Have you had any particularly good or bad experiences working in groups?

Mm, not really ‘cos like last year when we did a group course work we didn’t really take it seriously ‘cos we didn’t know what he really wanted but this year, because we know the rules and we know how things work, I think this year we’re alright – we’ve like taken it really seriously and we all want to do well and stuff like that. So not really – ‘cos like last year everything was just new to us – we didn’t know what to do or how to do it or – so it was just trial and error. This year it’s like get it right first go, so no I haven’t had any problems, at the moment. Well, there’s another – like my other group coursework that we’re having trouble in there, ‘cos one person isn’t doing the work – we’ve been having to carry them along, but apart from that – well, we just said we’ll do ours – we’ll have to do it for him and then just get him – get some marks knocked off his work.

Interviewer:	You said that you probably don’t always get on with the girls on the course – did you expect that at all when you started or did you think that because there weren’t many girls on the course, that you’d all stick together or..?

No, ‘cos what happened like – when I first came here for like my open day, I was – I think there was only about 5 girls I saw here and those 5 girls were the ones that have come on the course at the moment. I wasn’t – because their interests are different – they’re seriously into aircraft and they’re like if they spot a plane, they know which one it is and they’re like oh, I don’t know anything (laughter). I’m just like, oh really, is that what it is? I don’t – I can’t really like - so I’m not as interested, or as keen as them ‘cos they all want to go to flying and stuff like that and I’m not – for me it’s all about managing. I really – I wanted to do something – my career aspiration is like going to [airport] or wherever - sit there in the office and actually manage the airport. And that’s what I want to do, so I don’t really see myself being able to – I don’t – I actually make that interest because a lot of them are not too interested in terms of like stuff like that. They’re doing flying and stuff, I’m more into getting things sorted and having them working in their proper order and stuff like that. 

Interviewer:	So it’s more to do with personality than the fact they’re male or female?

Yeah, yeah, I think it is personality that dominates quite a bit and I think the other – I lied before – my other reason for not doing a placement is ‘cos all my mates that I hang around with at the moment, they’re not going on placement. It’s like – I don’t want to stick around and be left around with the other people, so that’s the other reason too – ‘cos I think the main – other than that – that wasn’t the main factor though, but…

Interviewer:	You were saying about your career aspirations a bit ago. So where do you see yourself in 5 years time?

5 years time? Erm, I probably won’t know working – basically, being in an office, like where I can see the runway or something, and just like working in a team with other people and just making things work. Making it really hectic – I really want it like – really like – not stressful, but I kind of – I want it to be a job where I don’t sit down, even for one second and I was just working all the time and I don’t mind the timings and stuff like that. I wouldn’t mind working from 11 till whatever time or 2 in the morning, till whatever time – I’m not fussed like that. I – I don’t know, yeah, something like that.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you’ll encounter any difficulties trying to achieve your career?

I probably will if I er – I don’t know. It depends on where I go and how I go about with my life, so if I like get married or something and then that’s a bit different. I think marriage is – could be a big difference in life, especially the ladies, like it’s very different.

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s because of your culture?

Yeah, my culture plays a massive part in my life – ‘cos it’s so different – and it depends at the moment, so…

Interviewer:	I think you mentioned a bit about this earlier, but do you think that the career prospects are good in your field of engineering?

I think they are – like not that bad. It’s like – if you were like successful then I’m sure you could get in. It’s not the fact that you’re male you get in or that they prefer male or anything, it’s nothing to do with that at the moment, so – I think there is, if you get the right person. It’s like getting to know the right person or anything. If you’ve got the contacts then you’re fine with it, so. It’s just about researching around and that’s the hard bit, and that’s where people like all the time - ‘cos it’s like putting all that effort in looking for a person, looking for a job. So I don’t think, at the moment – ‘cos my last resort would be basically working as a customer service – I would still go for that first and then work up through there, if I have to but that’d be my last resort. Obviously I don’t expect to come out of Uni and straight, go into management or anything, but I do see myself even working as a secretary in an airport, I’m happy with that as a first thing, and then move up from there – definite. After this, I really want to do air traffic control anyway, so – ‘cos that’s my first thing. That’s the only reason why I actually really like this job, because of air traffic control but because I can’t get in, I’m having trouble with it.

Interviewer:	Do you think that doing this degree will help you get in?

Not really because I – you don’t really need a degree to go on that course, ‘cos it’s just once you’re 18, if you pass their tests you’re fine with it and I only did a degree because I had to wait for a year. You can only apply, after a year, so I thought I’m not wasting the year – ‘cos of my age – my age is like – I’m one of the youngest people, so if I could finish – I finish before I’m even 21 – Uni, so I thought I don’t want to waste my year and stuff, so I thought I might as well just go to Uni now because I just left it to chance. But if I get air traffic control, I’ll go to there – if I get into Uni – I got into Uni – so whatever it was. I’m like that and I did get so many letters like oh, apply to this and apply to that but I wouldn’t take it, so this was my only choice.

Interviewer:	How do you think that when you do start work it’ll differ from being at university?

I guess it’s – it would be – I think it would still be the same. I don’t – ‘cos you’ll always be like doing a course, or doing this or doing that. You’ll always be working to go up all the time, so it’s not really different. But the only difference would be like at the moment, I go home and chill out – probably I’ll be like working there and then come in at night and go to Uni or like go to study and I think that’s the only difference really like. But then you’ve also got like social part anyway, so I don’t think it’s really different. 

Interviewer:	Do you think that you’ll get treated differently?

I don’t think – again, in terms of our society it’s different because in here I can do – I can come in when ever I want. If I don’t want to go to lectures, I can miss the lectures – obviously you can’t do that, and time constraints and stuff like that, but I think it’ll work, during summer and stuff and I won’t have to get into time and get out of times. I’m used to that, it’s not that I haven’t been used to like waking up at 6 O’clock in the morning, or whatever, I’m alright with that. So, no – I don’t think it is…

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think that you’ll take from your course into work – like in terms of skills and things like that?

Probably – I have learnt quite a lot. I definitely have. Some of the things I didn’t really know, that I’ve learnt. So it’s quite good like in terms of like that – they taught us quite a diversity of things ‘cos it wasn’t just airlines and it wasn’t aircraft. You needed other knowledge to get into like – stuff like policies and stuff, ideas really, ‘cos you’re taught that this affects this and economics affects like that and I guess I have broadened up a bit, from the knowledge of just airlines and aircraft so I have broadened up – definitely – apart from the fact that it’s not just all to do with that and you have to know about other parts of management and finance and – I don’t think – it’s just like – it has taught me quite a bit like – in terms of like that you need a wide knowledge and stuff like that.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the group work and things like that, that you’ve done will help in…?

I think it will – definite – ‘cos like it’s all about like managing the group and making sure like they do their own bit and you do yours, and getting it all together and stuff. It is, I think, a learning process – ‘cos obviously when you’re out at work, you’re all working as a team it’s not really one person running the whole thing. So, definite, yeah.

Interviewer:	What do you think will be the best things and the worst things about working?

Er, the best thing would be like, just being there and – ‘cos that’s the final goal of life, isn’t it? You want to be working and earning, so I think the best thing would be like just being there, in the final stage of your life. So by working – I think if you’ve got a job, you’ve got so much status and so you’ve achieved your status, whatever the job it is, but you’ve achieved your status, and obviously you can go higher and higher but I think the good thing is that you’ve got a job, you’re secured in terms of everything like. Because nowadays people look for everything don’t they? You have to have a job, you have to have a house. Everything – you can start building your life now, once you’ve got a job. I think the down side would be like – I don’t think there is a down side to it, really ‘cos at the end of the day – I guess, if you get bored of it, then it’s a bit thingy but if you like keep on just moving up or changing, like in air transport I was always told that you can move – like can move all round, wherever you want to go. So in terms of my field, I think I’m alright with it, so if I got bored with one thing I could probably move up. Like even in terms of air traffic control, like I could like 5 years or 10 years and then I can end up teaching if I want. turns.text: You said that you probably don’t always get on with the girls on the course – did you expect that at all when you started or did you think that because there weren’t many girls on the course, that you’d all stick together or..?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, ‘cos what happened like – when I first came here for like my open day, I was – I think there was only about 5 girls I saw here and those 5 girls were the ones that have come on the course at the moment. I wasn’t – because their interests are different – they’re seriously into aircraft and they’re like if they spot a plane, they know which one it is and they’re like oh, I don’t know anything (laughter). I’m just like, oh really, is that what it is? I don’t – I can’t really like - so I’m not as interested, or as keen as them ‘cos they all want to go to flying and stuff like that and I’m not – for me it’s all about managing. I really – I wanted to do something – my career aspiration is like going to [airport] or wherever - sit there in the office and actually manage the airport. And that’s what I want to do, so I don’t really see myself being able to – I don’t – I actually make that interest because a lot of them are not too interested in terms of like stuff like that. They’re doing flying and stuff, I’m more into getting things sorted and having them working in their proper order and stuff like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So it’s more to do with personality than the fact they’re male or female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah, I think it is personality that dominates quite a bit and I think the other – I lied before – my other reason for not doing a placement is ‘cos all my mates that I hang around with at the moment, they’re not going on placement. It’s like – I don’t want to stick around and be left around with the other people, so that’s the other reason too – ‘cos I think the main – other than that – that wasn’t the main factor though, but…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You were saying about your career aspirations a bit ago. So where do you see yourself in 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: 5 years time? Erm, I probably won’t know working – basically, being in an office, like where I can see the runway or something, and just like working in a team with other people and just making things work. Making it really hectic – I really want it like – really like – not stressful, but I kind of – I want it to be a job where I don’t sit down, even for one second and I was just working all the time and I don’t mind the timings and stuff like that. I wouldn’t mind working from 11 till whatever time or 2 in the morning, till whatever time – I’m not fussed like that. I – I don’t know, yeah, something like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you’ll encounter any difficulties trying to achieve your career?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I probably will if I er – I don’t know. It depends on where I go and how I go about with my life, so if I like get married or something and then that’s a bit different. I think marriage is – could be a big difference in life, especially the ladies, like it’s very different.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that’s because of your culture?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, my culture plays a massive part in my life – ‘cos it’s so different – and it depends at the moment, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I think you mentioned a bit about this earlier, but do you think that the career prospects are good in your field of engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think they are – like not that bad. It’s like – if you were like successful then I’m sure you could get in. It’s not the fact that you’re male you get in or that they prefer male or anything, it’s nothing to do with that at the moment, so – I think there is, if you get the right person. It’s like getting to know the right person or anything. If you’ve got the contacts then you’re fine with it, so. It’s just about researching around and that’s the hard bit, and that’s where people like all the time - ‘cos it’s like putting all that effort in looking for a person, looking for a job. So I don’t think, at the moment – ‘cos my last resort would be basically working as a customer service – I would still go for that first and then work up through there, if I have to but that’d be my last resort. Obviously I don’t expect to come out of Uni and straight, go into management or anything, but I do see myself even working as a secretary in an airport, I’m happy with that as a first thing, and then move up from there – definite. After this, I really want to do air traffic control anyway, so – ‘cos that’s my first thing. That’s the only reason why I actually really like this job, because of air traffic control but because I can’t get in, I’m having trouble with it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that doing this degree will help you get in?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really because I – you don’t really need a degree to go on that course, ‘cos it’s just once you’re 18, if you pass their tests you’re fine with it and I only did a degree because I had to wait for a year. You can only apply, after a year, so I thought I’m not wasting the year – ‘cos of my age – my age is like – I’m one of the youngest people, so if I could finish – I finish before I’m even 21 – Uni, so I thought I don’t want to waste my year and stuff, so I thought I might as well just go to Uni now because I just left it to chance. But if I get air traffic control, I’ll go to there – if I get into Uni – I got into Uni – so whatever it was. I’m like that and I did get so many letters like oh, apply to this and apply to that but I wouldn’t take it, so this was my only choice.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you think that when you do start work it’ll differ from being at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I guess it’s – it would be – I think it would still be the same. I don’t – ‘cos you’ll always be like doing a course, or doing this or doing that. You’ll always be working to go up all the time, so it’s not really different. But the only difference would be like at the moment, I go home and chill out – probably I’ll be like working there and then come in at night and go to Uni or like go to study and I think that’s the only difference really like. But then you’ve also got like social part anyway, so I don’t think it’s really different.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you’ll get treated differently?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t think – again, in terms of our society it’s different because in here I can do – I can come in when ever I want. If I don’t want to go to lectures, I can miss the lectures – obviously you can’t do that, and time constraints and stuff like that, but I think it’ll work, during summer and stuff and I won’t have to get into time and get out of times. I’m used to that, it’s not that I haven’t been used to like waking up at 6 O’clock in the morning, or whatever, I’m alright with that. So, no – I don’t think it is…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think that you’ll take from your course into work – like in terms of skills and things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Probably – I have learnt quite a lot. I definitely have. Some of the things I didn’t really know, that I’ve learnt. So it’s quite good like in terms of like that – they taught us quite a diversity of things ‘cos it wasn’t just airlines and it wasn’t aircraft. You needed other knowledge to get into like – stuff like policies and stuff, ideas really, ‘cos you’re taught that this affects this and economics affects like that and I guess I have broadened up a bit, from the knowledge of just airlines and aircraft so I have broadened up – definitely – apart from the fact that it’s not just all to do with that and you have to know about other parts of management and finance and – I don’t think – it’s just like – it has taught me quite a bit like – in terms of like that you need a wide knowledge and stuff like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the group work and things like that, that you’ve done will help in…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it will – definite – ‘cos like it’s all about like managing the group and making sure like they do their own bit and you do yours, and getting it all together and stuff. It is, I think, a learning process – ‘cos obviously when you’re out at work, you’re all working as a team it’s not really one person running the whole thing. So, definite, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think will be the best things and the worst things about working?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, the best thing would be like, just being there and – ‘cos that’s the final goal of life, isn’t it? You want to be working and earning, so I think the best thing would be like just being there, in the final stage of your life. So by working – I think if you’ve got a job, you’ve got so much status and so you’ve achieved your status, whatever the job it is, but you’ve achieved your status, and obviously you can go higher and higher but I think the good thing is that you’ve got a job, you’re secured in terms of everything like. Because nowadays people look for everything don’t they? You have to have a job, you have to have a house. Everything – you can start building your life now, once you’ve got a job. I think the down side would be like – I don’t think there is a down side to it, really ‘cos at the end of the day – I guess, if you get bored of it, then it’s a bit thingy but if you like keep on just moving up or changing, like in air transport I was always told that you can move – like can move all round, wherever you want to go. So in terms of my field, I think I’m alright with it, so if I got bored with one thing I could probably move up. Like even in terms of air traffic control, like I could like 5 years or 10 years and then I can end up teaching if I want. So, it’s not just that I’m going to be stuck with that, I could try and do like – retire in terms of like step down, work in just the aerodrome area or just like, funnily enough – it’s not that it’s really limited in the way that – I don’t – I don’t think. I guess the only difference would be like if you had like a family problem or something so otherwise I don’t think working has got a down side really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that your course or your university experience prepares you for going out into the workplace?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it does – definite. I guess if I did have a placement, it would be good. It would be really nice because I’d come out with one year’s experience and I would be more attractive than someone who hasn’t done it, but at the end of the day, it’s like getting it in the first place – and er – but yeah, definite – at least you’ve got that knowledge, like you’re not going into it – like if I was going into an airline – if I’d did a degree in airline and I was going into computing, then I don’t have no knowledge of that so like this way at least if I want – because I want to go into airlines, at least that will give me a basic to it. At least I’ve got the foundations, so I think it will help and like, obviously it will help me in terms of like where I want to go, what I want to do and stuff, ‘cos some of the things I didn’t even know existed in the first place so obviously you’ve got that. University definitely does prepare you for it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far? Would you do anything differently if you went through it all again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, no. I think I’d go to the same – I’d seriously do the same.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s good. What 5 words would you use to describe the culture or the characteristics of the engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Ha, er 5 words

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It doesn’t matter if you can’t think of 5 words exactly but…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, it’s still a hard question. What do you mean by culture or…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Oh like would you – like…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Characteristics of work (yeah). Er, I would say dynamic, erm, it’s a really hard one. Mm, (pause)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it is masculine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I don’t think that. I think a girl could go to a construction site and do this stuff. I don’t think, in terms of that, it is that, but I guess you need – again you need like the dynamic part of it, you need the – you need your – I don’t know – would you say interest in it. I’ve lost my words.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I suppose you’re were saying earlier about being imaginative.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah stuff like that. I guess you do need to be creative and you need that part of you, in there so. You also need to be strong –to do like – being able to wake up like at 6 in the morning, and 2 in the morning and basically have will power and stuff like that and that really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there’s anything about the engineering culture that will cause you any problems?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. I think that’ll probably push me more forward, because honestly I didn’t know that transport was part of engineering and stuff. I think it gives a different perspective to it. It makes it more technical like, it seems like oh shit, it’s technical isn’t it. So I don’t know I think it’ll probably push it, I’ll be more respected by other people, ‘cos if I say I’m from the engineering department, or something like that. I could be able to go into engineering – I think it’d probably push it that, give me more – (?) or something.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you think that your educational experiences differ from say someone in social sciences or business school or something like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm, not really because like I say our course isn’t going out and doing surveying or anything. So I can’t say it’s different – it’d probably be the same as managing a business but I know it’s different in terms of computing and stuff ‘cos they actually go out and making programmes – so it’s different in that way but I guess we do the same. We do stuff like making an airline, an air – you go around learning about aircraft and stuff, so it’s not really different in that way, no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s about all I have for you, I don’t know if you want to say…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No I don’t have anything to say I hope I’ve said…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: No it’s good, you’ve been an enormous help, thank you.
